faq.a: VIA gives immediate visual results, requires no laboratory, and allows same‑day treatment.
faq.q: Why is VIA used instead of Pap smear in many low‑resource settings?

faq.q: Can a normal CA‑125 rule out ovarian cancer?

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with post‑coital bleeding; what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform VIA or Pap smear; HIV increases risk of high‑grade CIN, early detection is critical.

A patient with a 10‑cm pelvic mass and anemia is scheduled for surgery; what intra‑operative assessment determines malignancy? — Inspect for surface implants, ascites, and obtain frozen section; guides extent of resection.

How would you manage a tubo‑ovarian abscess when CT is unavailable? — Start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering Gram‑negative and anaerobes; monitor clinically and consider bedside drainage if no improvement.

Explain why levonorgestrel IUS is preferred over oral progestins for endometrial hyperplasia in a low‑resource clinic. — Provides high local dose with minimal systemic side effects and requires only one insertion.
A woman with chronic pelvic pain has a normal ultrasound; what condition should you still consider and what test helps? — Endometriosis; diagnostic laparoscopy with visual inspection and biopsy.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with known cervical cancer indicates possible fistula formation? — Passage of urine or feces through the vagina; requires imaging and surgical referral.
Why is a negative Pap smear insufficient in a woman with persistent vaginal ulcer? — Ulcer may be due to non‑cervical malignancy or infection; biopsy of the lesion is required.

In a resource‑limited setting, how would you screen for ovarian cancer in a high‑risk BRCA carrier? — Annual trans‑vaginal ultrasound combined with clinical pelvic exam; CA‑125 may be used if affordable.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A systematic approach to common female reproductive diseases in low‑resource settings, focusing on diagnosis, staging, causes, investigations and management for ward‑round practice.

b: Identify the organ involved by targeted history and exam.
Use WHO or FIGO criteria for cancer staging when applicable.
sections.p: Female reproductive pathology encompasses any disease of the vulva, vagina, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes or ovaries, including pregnancy‑related disorders.

b: Early stage (FIGO I‑II) often curable with surgery alone.
Advanced stage (FIGO III‑IV) needs multimodal therapy.
sections.p: Severity is graded by organ‑specific systems: FIGO stage for cervical/uterine cancer, WHO grade for endometriosis, and WHO classification for ovarian tumours.

b: Infections: HIV‑related cervical dysplasia, TB salpingitis, schistosomiasis‑associated squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder (adjacent to cervix).
Hormonal: Polycystic ovary syndrome, prolonged estrogen exposure leading to endometrial hyperplasia.
Genetic/Hereditary: BRCA‑related ovarian cancer, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive ovarian infarction.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common aetiologies are infectious, hormonal, and hereditary.

b: Vulvar ulcer or mass with foul discharge – think malignancy or ulcerative STI.
Post‑coital bleeding – cervical lesion.
Pelvic pain + irregular bleeding – fibroids, endometriosis, or ovarian tumour.
Acute abdomen with fever – tubo‑ovarian abscess or ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
sections.p: Presentations vary by organ but share red‑flag symptoms that prompt urgent evaluation.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there a visible lesion or discharge? Positive finding directs biopsy or treatment.

t.a: Pap smear (or VIA in low‑resource settings)
t.b: Screen for cervical intra‑epithelial neoplasia; VIA positive → immediate cryotherapy if histology unavailable.
What is the size, location and nature of a pelvic mass? Solid mass → suspect malignancy; cystic → likely functional cyst.
Is there a marker suggestive of epithelial ovarian cancer? Elevated supports malignancy but is non‑specific.
Does immunosuppression contribute to cervical disease? Positive → intensified surveillance.
Is there hyperplasia or carcinoma? Positive histology guides definitive therapy.

b: Severe anemia from chronic bleeding.
Rapidly enlarging pelvic mass with systemic signs – possible ovarian cancer.
Fever, foul discharge, and peritoneal signs – tubo‑ovarian abscess rupture.
Persistent post‑coital bleeding – advanced cervical cancer.
sections.p: Recognise signs that indicate imminent danger or irreversible damage.

b: Infection: Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑cloxacillin) for tubo‑ovarian abscess; add metronidazole for anaerobes.
Cancer: Surgery (hysterectomy, salpingo‑oophorectomy) for early stage; add radiotherapy/chemotherapy for advanced disease.
Benign tumours: Myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation for fibroids; hormonal therapy (levonorgestrel IUS) for endometrial hyperplasia.
Pregnancy‑related pathology: Immediate referral for ectopic pregnancy or severe pre‑eclampsia.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications.

b: Annual VIA or Pap smear for women >30, especially HIV‑positive.
Post‑treatment ultrasound at 6 weeks and then every 6 months for ovarian tumour survivors.
HPV vaccination where available; safe sexual practices.
sections.p: Long‑term surveillance reduces recurrence and mortality.

b: Pelvic inflammatory disease vs. ectopic pregnancy – use pregnancy test and ultrasound.
Endometriosis vs. adenomyosis – MRI or histology differentiates.
Fibroids vs. ovarian cysts – location on ultrasound distinguishes.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic common female reproductive diseases.

b: Pap smear may miss glandular lesions; consider colposcopy if suspicion remains.
CA‑125 can be raised in benign conditions (endometriosis, pelvic TB).
Ultrasound may underestimate depth of cervical invasion; MRI is superior if available.
sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe pelvic pain with fever
Rapidly enlarging pelvic mass with weight loss
Persistent abnormal vaginal discharge despite antibiotics
